utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the proceedings. Appearing for Mr. Perisic are Mr. Lukic and Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pardon. Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. The microphone is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just to remind you, Mr. Novakovic, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic, how much more time are you still going to be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole of today's day and a part of tomorrow. I can provide an additional explanation for that, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to warn you that you are very close on to the time-limit that you had given, and the Trial Chamber is concerned about the time consumed in presenting the evidence, and, in fact, the Trial Chamber has sought that your attention be drawn to the provisions of Rule 90 so that now henceforth as you go along you bear them in mind. 90(F). You are aware of it? I can read them to you: "The Trial Chamber shall exercise the control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to, A, make the interrogation and present for effective for the ascertainment of truth; and, B, avoid needless consumption of time." So please bear that in mind. The Trial Chamber has been warning you about this but has been fairly lenient and the intention is to be a little more strict about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully believe that you are going to -- I'm going to reserve, but Honourable Judge Moloto, may I indicate several factors which brought me into such a situation with this witness and why I think that his examination should be conducted within this framework. One of the reasons is when we drafted our summary for this witness and estimated the time necessary for him, as I recall, we estimated around three days being necessary, at that time we did not have in our possession the so-called additional material disclosed subsequently, meaning General Mladic's diary. And in this respect, I focused with this witness only on three entries in those diaries which I deem material for these proceedings, as you saw yesterday, and I'm going to conduct the interrogation in such a manner today, is to focus only on those things which help illuminate the matters for the benefit of the bench. The second reason is what has already been the position of the Defence during the presentation of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution adduce some 1500 documents in the courtroom without them being adduced through witnesses. We have not had a single viva voce word being said about those documents, and it's been left to you, the Bench, to rely on those exhibits and what is written in those documents, to draw your own conclusions. But among those there are many documents which directly speak about the issues that this witness can testify about and, what is more important, they are documents authored by this witness. For you to get a full picture, I believe that 25 reports have been adduced as special P exhibits by the Prosecution concerning reports from commander of the SVK to President Milosevic, and you have not heard a single word of testimony about those, and the rules and the guide-lines determine what is a priority way of establishing facts. My intention has always been, and the gist of what I'm saying, is to go through certain documents with this witness which are P exhibits, exhibits of the Prosecution. Through this witness, I've adduced only a handful of Defence exhibits. My intention is to work on Prosecution exhibits that we have not had testimony about in this courtroom. If the Bench believe that my questions fall outside the framework of what is necessary to determine the facts, I'm in your hands and you may of course ban any such questions. What I've asked the question and what I intend to ask the question -- the witness is I believe essential for these proceedings. Finally, we are going to give up some witnesses from our 65 ter list if we are able to fully use this witness to be more economical. This is the first witness testifying about the SVK and could prove to be the only witness discussing this matter in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. Let me just say for the record, Mr. Lukic, that in fact none of the points that you raise is a concern of the Chamber with respect to consumption of time. The concern of the Chamber is that starting with you, you preface your questions with a whole long background. Yesterday, I pointed to you that you spoke for two-thirds of the screen only to then put one little question at the end which didn't need any background information whatsoever. Similarly your witness does the same, not only this one, most of them have been doing that. I'm asking you to, one, control yourself; two, control the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understood your instructions and I'll do my best to follow them. Thank you. Let's go back to the document that we discussed with the witness concerning the 8th of November, 1993, meeting at the Presidency of Serbia. Since we could not resolve the technical problems, we've prepared, Your Honours, copies of the document. I would like the Serbian version to be placed on the ELMO, if possible. We are supposed to receive additional hard copies for you any moment. For the time being I've just got one paper copy for your benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before starting with the document, General, let me ask you a question. As far as we can see, this reflects the third such visit that you had with General Mladic and General Perisic. To the best of your recollection, I'd like to find out what was the behaviour and conduct of General Perisic at such joint meetings at the time at the beginning of his career as Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall is that Mr. Perisic conducted in a very reserved manner at those meetings. He spoke very generally about what General Staff of the VJ knew about the enemy, about the other elements, about the condition within the VJ with a focus on logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have one copy for the General to keep in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you have a copy in front of you. Could you please turn to page 3. We'll wait for the other participants in the courtroom to do likewise. What I'd like to hear is the bottom part of the document, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friends, where we left off yesterday is page 3 of the document at the place where at the bottom of the document, at the bottom of the page you see a line saying "General Perisic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then let me turn another page, I'd like to hear your comment, General, and we are not going to focus on the first entry but what is the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could turn to the next page on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "We must ensure united platform for waging a war." General, does this trigger your memory as to the actual words of General Perisic at that meeting, and what was it all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall what General Perisic said and this does remind me of what he said at that meeting. The essence of this entry to secure or ensure a united platform for waging a war is -- was in essence his request that the basic united platform be created and the one without which everything else is irrelevant is the funding of the army for the army to have what it needs for waging a war in terms of materiel, supplies, et cetera. This is how I understood his words. Because, first and foremost, of the situation in the VJ, and then but not as the most important thing in the armies of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom it is said: "The army has done the following: 1, we have determined our western borders. The FRY has been created and lives in peace." And under 3: "The army is resilient. It is an effective organ." Do you recall what Mr. Perisic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember perfectly because the context of his words and his intervention were clear to me. As you saw, state organ representatives attended the meeting, both of Republic of Serbia, the most important figures from Republika Srpska, and representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. From the outset, I understood that General Perisic was conducting an argument with some leaders from Republic of Serbia. There was a certain dose of rivalry between the army, the government, state security, those most important institutions. Who did what, who was good, who was bad, and why they were bad and why somebody who is good was good. So when General Perisic states here that we've determined our western borders and when he refers to the army, I'm not sure whether he said "we determined" or "we've done our work concerning the western borders," he refers to the VJ [as interpreted]. He did take part in the western-most part of the front line as an officer of the JNA. And he is discussing the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 7, line 12, he referred to the Yugoslav People's Army, and the transcript reflects the words VJ. I do believe that the witness said the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just have the witness confirm that, as opposed to Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still trying to find out exactly where we are. We were supposed to be on page 3, Mr. Lukic says we are now going to page 7. I've tried to go four pages forward, so I seed to see that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Lukic, I think, was referring to the transcript page 7 as opposed to the diary entry page 7. He was directing the witness's attention and the court's attention to page 7, my line 12, where the letters VJ is noted. My request is that the witness confirm what his language was as opposed to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, part of your answer said: "So when General Perisic states here that we've determined our western borders and when he refers to the army, I'm not sure whether he said 'we determined' or 'we've done our work concerning the western borders,' he refers to..." can you mention the name of the army that he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. General Perisic here had in mind the Yugoslav People's Army. And when he spoke about the western borders, he was referring to what the JNA had done in the conflicts during 1991 because the VJ as an army did not participate in anything concerning any western borders, be it RSK or the RS. Later on in my reply, I continued and I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. All we wanted to know is you said the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, just a bit ago you mentioned the rivalry that existed within the various establishments of authorities of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you know which authorities within the FRY Milosevic respected best?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, Mr. Milosevic had most respect for his political party and people from his political party which was the Socialist Party of Serbia. And then after that in this period of time, I think that he had more respect for the state security than for the army. That was the feeling that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 where the words of General Perisic are presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's page 4 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says under item 2: "The FRY has been created and lives in peace." Do you see that bit? What is the meaning of these words of General Perisic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what General Perisic said. This was his statement concerning how he saw this as one of the great achievements that had been accomplished until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the first bit on this page seem to be the words of Prime Minister Sainovic. In his second sentence, as is presented in the document, he says: "It is not yet time to speak about merits, and I would say this to General Perisic." Do you have recollection of these words of Prime Minister Sainovic in this context as is presented here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was this discussion that was somewhat concealed at the highest level -- conducted at the highest level between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Perisic. Mr. Sainovic obviously thought that he had to prevent General Perisic from scoring a point in presenting what the army, as one of the structures of the government, the VJ, had done up until that time from 1991 until this time which was October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One intervention -- two interventions. Can you give us the reference page, the page reference where you say -- you said we must go one page forward, and I don't see any Sainovic talking there. Number one. Nor do I see the quotation that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4. On page 4 you see the name Sainovic and then if you turn to page 5, the second entry, the second line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we are aligned, Mr. Lukic. The document I have starts at page 19, the pagination on the document. Can we use that pagination. Is it page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 23. I don't have Sainovic talking at all. Even on page 22. Okay. Now I see him. Now, where is it where he says it is not, what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the fact that our work is complicated when it comes to hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's understandable, Mr. Lukic. It's not your fault, it's the system that is broken down. Just before this disappears, if you look at page 9, line 24, again the interpretation talks of the VJ had done up until that time from 1991. Now, in 1991 there was no VJ. Now, I want to find out whether the witness said the VJ or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, will you please repeat what you said, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the army as an institution had done, that is to say the JNA in the conflicts in 1991 and in 1992. I meant army as an institution, as one of the state institutions. I have not mentioned the VJ, Your Honours. At the time it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Well, the interpretation mentioned the VJ. May I again ask then the interpreters to -- we realise all of us that it is important to distinguish between the JNA and the VJ and to the extent necessary between the VRS and the SVK, so let's listen to the testimony carefully and if the witness says JNA, let us note that he said JNA and translate it as such. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A bit lower down under item 5 we see the words uttered by Martic at the time. Could you please comment on them. On the second sentence, which you can see before you, Your Honours, where it is stated that he had said: "We should have a united army." And then "(the FRY, RS and the RSK) and the same should be done with the police." And then below that it says: "We should have one state security." Based on your recollection, is this what Mr. Martic said at the time and was there any reaction, if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Martic said that at the time, and there was no particular reaction to what he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on was a united army and united police force created or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to skip over the words of Mr. Karadzic, and then on the following page, Your Honours, we see once again the words uttered by President Milosevic, which is at the bottom of page 24 and then goes on to page 25. Here it says: "We have been working for weeks trying to set up a meeting with the Muslims. RS has become reality to end the war in Bosnia as soon as possible." And then on the following page it says: "The Croatian-Muslim issue will come to surface and so will the Serbian-Croatian issue. Try to organise a secret Serbian Muslim meeting in Thessaloniki. Papandreou has already undertaken specific steps in this regard." General, what can you tell us about this entry?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Milosevic said this because for me this was something completely new, something I hadn't known until that time. In explaining this position of his, he said that it was necessary to achieve piece with the Muslims. That's how he put it. He also anticipated a possibility - on the second page we can see that - of a Croatian-Muslim conflict. At the time he said that he was trying to organise a meeting between Serbs and Muslims via Greek diplomats and officials, a meeting that would lead to -- that would help end the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A bit lower, General, under item 11, we have something concerning you, and this entry is a bit unclear so I will ask you, do you remember what you said at the meeting? Do you remember what this entry is all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I requested what I needed in order to organise defence in the eastern part for the 11th Corps, and I thought that in order to organise defence in normal defence, we would need additional two tank companies and one support division, artillery division.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive that later on; did you get that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't because they said to me that should I really need that, perhaps these forces could enter that area during the conflict, at the time of the conflict, and that deployment of that military equipment at that point in time would be politically dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this something that was not noted in this minute, or is there anything in the minutes here under Mr. Milosevic that points to that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this entry here in the diaries, only the words -- only part of the words I uttered are reflected. They wrote down what it is that I requested and not the reasons for me requesting that. And as for Mr. Milosevic, he said that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He didn't say it in response to you right here when you were making this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At such meetings it wasn't customary, Your Honours, to give responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So he didn't give you an answer at that time? Just say yes or no. Very well, I understand. He will give the answer when his turn comes to speak. It's just that his turn came to speak immediately after you here, and I would have thought that you would respond to your request and what you tell us he told you would have been minuted. Okay. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now skip the next part and then move to the bottom of page 26, Your Honours. And again we see the words of President Milosevic under item 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the second sentence he says: "We will draw conclusions that we will send to you while the conduct of this leadership..." I don't know whether this can help you refresh your memory, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what Mr. Milosevic said, that they would draw up the conclusions that they would send to us, which is to say that he took it upon himself to do this together with his closest associates, to draw up these conclusions. And when he says this leadership, he was referring to the people who were at that meeting in a leadership capacity, and also about the responsibility of these people at the meeting whom he was referring to as the leadership. Whereas I saw it as a sort of a temporary working organ, and when it comes to the responsibility of this leadership, you see that he did not complete the sentence, there are three dots, but he was referring to the people who were present there at the meeting who were there in a leadership capacity and who were to abide by the conclusions that were yet to be drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then the bit that comes underneath it, under item 1 and then all the way down to item 10. We don't need to discuss all of this, but under item 1 it says: "Start compiling a single war plan and define how to continue waging the war, a single plan for all three armies."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood this at the time as a first topic for those forthcoming conclusions whose contents were supposed to be what is jotted down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to discuss a document shortly -- well, let me ask you, was there a single war plan being drafted after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a single war plan labelled "Drina" was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the single plan to continue waging the war was -- this single plan for all the three armies, did it ever come to fruition, was it ever defined?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document as the highest synthesis at the very highest level enumerating the war goals and objectives, political and other resources, the military doctrine and the military strategies, such a document was never defined on the Serb side, and serious people and individual say that this was one of the major failures of all the Serb leaderships. Such things were never defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention concerning the transcript. On page 15, line 13 concerning my question, which is based on what is written here, the witness's answer, the first word in his answer was "ratovodstvo" or plan to wage the war, or waging the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To clarify those terms, let me ask you this, General. Is there a difference between a war plan and "ratovodstvo" or war waging plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "ratovodstvo" is a much broader term which encompasses both political goals and diplomatic goals and military goals. Whereas war plan is just an individual technical document for the carrying out of what represents a military activity within this "ratovodstvo" or a broader war-waging plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I make also an intervention. On the same page, 15, at line 16 you say "such a document was never defined on the Serb side." What do you mean by the "Serb side"? That's how you were translated or interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't referring to a document, Your Honours. I discussed a concept of war waging as a notion, as an effort to define war goals and involvement of political, diplomatic, economic, and military resources to achieve those goals, and I also said that such a defined concept of war waging, or "ratovodstvo" was never defined on the Serb side. There were ad hoc decision, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is what do you mean by "on the Serb side"? Who are you referring to when you say "the Serb side"? There are Serbs in the Krajina, there are Serbs in Serbia, there are Serbs in the Republika Srpska, there are Serbs -- I'm not quite sure who you are talking about. Are you talk that the Serb people of former Yugoslavia, all of them, wherever they are, didn't define this concept in their minds, it was only defined by the Croats and the Muslims, or do you mean by the Serb side a particular area, particular entity, particular community? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mean those people attending this meeting, state leaderships of Serbia, Republika Srpska, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina who are discussing direction of war and whereas basic principles of waging the war were never defined. Mr. Milosevic said this is a united leadership, a single leadership, but this was not true, simply it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe we could take a break at this stage, I know we started late but just so that we synchronise with time. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I am going to continue on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for your benefit, Your Honours, that would be page 27 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just the last entry, General, under 9 it says: "Put together a programme regarding traffic, how to enable this and RH to the extent that it does not threaten RSK interests." Could you please comment just this entry as reflected here under item 9?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic uttered those words, and this was not the only one that he said something to that effect. This entry contains his position that Republic of Croatia should be allowed or enabled, and that would naturally be achieved through certain negotiations, to communicate with those parts of the territory with which communication had been disrupted because we held under our control parts of the territory through which those lines of communications passed. First and foremost, this refers to those roads and other communication lines through Western Slavonia and communications with Dalmatia, southern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We may continue. What was Mr. Milosevic's interest in holding such a position at the time, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such his opinion coincides with all his other positions expressed at the time that in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and in the Republika Srpska a peaceful process should be conducted. On the other hand, he -- to the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina he suggested that it would be in their best interest to reduce tensions by allowing Croatia to maintain communications with all parts of its territory with continued existence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 29 now, and that would be the last page of the document. General, you see the third sentence. It is stated here: "A question as to giving instructions for RP, when should we put it together and everything which follows below." This is something I showed you in proofing. Could you please take a look at this entry and tell us whether this was another topic discussed then and whether this entry reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entry refers to what I remember to wit his guidance that Mr. Milosevic issued to the effect that the basic elements of the comment war plan that was supposed to be prepared should be put in place, and RP means "ratni plan" or war plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then subsequently, could you please read the entries until the end of the page, Saturday, 13th of November, meeting of the working party or team for putting together the RP, what is it all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those entries below the line above which reference is made to RP when should we put it together, that portion of the text is not what anybody at the meeting said. These are notes or aide-memoire to Mr. Mladic. He notes down tasks for himself about what he should be doing together with his Main Staff, and you see here it says, the 19th of November for the RP to be completed. In effect, he issues tasks to the Main Staff of the VRS to perform the elements of that joint war plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document and for it to be MFI'd for the time being until we've conducted certain verifications of the translation, at least of some parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D442.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, a minute ago you mentioned something and I'm going to ask you about that. Did you -- first of all, do you know what the Drina directive is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each war plan at the strategic level contains a general part which is labelled directive. Directives are drafted at the highest possible level at the General Staff level which means before drafting of the war plan started, and that a war plan was subsequently labelled Drina, the General Staff of the VJ, Main Staff of the VRS, and the Main Staff of the SVK had first to prepare the dispositional element of the plan, and that would be that directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid we will still bound to use the ELMO and the hard copies, although I do see something on the screen. P215, if we could have that put on the screen. I'm hopeful that the e-court is now functional since I see something on my screen, but in any case, I have a copy of paper versions of a part of P215 for your benefit. I didn't want to print everything, just the portion that we are going to work on with the witness, and that is the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you please in a couple of words say whether you took part in drafting this document? And if anybody else from the SVK took part, could you please indicate who?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you saw from the preceding document on page 29, General Mladic determined his team to work on preparing the war plan, first of all the directive. The same was done by me. When it comes to the Main Staff of the SVK, I nominated that working party. Me and my assistants took part in drafting the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe where was this document drafted, was it drafted separately or jointly, at which location?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment of the situation at the level of the RSK and the drafting of conclusions of the assessment and the basic elements for the directive were drafted in Knin. Harmonisation and the wording in drafting of the final version of the directive was done at the General Staff in the war room at the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, please turn to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this would be page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Heading "Ideas for Manoeuvres."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to discuss the second paragraph, if we could go up or down -- scroll down for the benefit of the witness, I'm interested in the last paragraph. The paragraph starts with the words: "In the case of an aggression of HV on the RSK." "In the event of HV aggression on the RSK." I'm not sure, I don't have an English version so this is why I'm saying this, I'm trying to give you reference points to the best of my recollection. If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The paragraph reads: "In the event of HV aggression on the RSK by the integrated use of armed forces of the Serbian people, decisive defence and offensive operations on the selected axes and regions of the RSK to crush the coalition forces in Dalmatia and the former BiH, as well as a possible armed rebellion in crisis regions of FRY, with the main VJ forces simultaneously preparing for the crushing of Ustasha and Muslim forces and the eventual termination of war." And then the next sentence states: "In the RSK, by decisive events prevent surprises and rapid and deep penetrations of the HV, while at the same time engaging parts of the VJ in Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem, and the VRS in Western Slavonia and Krajina, thus crushing the aggressors attack and creating conditions for offensive operations." General, when this document was being drafted, did you believe that what is written here will materialise in an event of an aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Mr. Lukic, it was difficult for me to believe something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did there come a time when there was aggression by the Republic of Croatia on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a general offensive that started on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there appears to be a missing portion of the text --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am sorry. There appears to be a missing portion of the text. In the English text, there is a portion in the first paragraph that was read by Mr. Lukic. The words on the third line of the English "defend the RSK." That appears to be the missing in the text of the transcript, and I think those are words that should not be -- if they exist, they should be incorporated into the transcript. It's on page 21, line 14, is where the transcript apparently omits the words "defend the RSK," so I'm trying to reconcile what is the text before me in English and what appears on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I notice that in fact there are words such as distortions in Dalmatia which are in the transcript which are not there in the text of this document. Maybe there was a mishearing here. Mr. Novakovic, if you could maybe just go through that paragraph one more time so that we can get it on the record correctly. You can just read it as it stands there so that it gets on correctly, and take it slowly so that the stenographer can keep pace with you. Starting "with in the event of HV aggression." Start there, just that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the event of the aggression of the Croatian army on the Republic of Serbian Krajina, by the integrated use of armed forces of the Serbian people, decisive defence and offensive operations on the selected axes and theatres defend the RSK, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, route or crush the coalition forces in Dalmatia and the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as a possible armed rebellion in the crisis region of the FRY with the main Yugoslav Army VJ forces simultaneously preparing for the crushing of Ustasha and Muslim forces and for the eventual termination of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I asked you if there was an aggression, you said that there was in August, and I put another question to you, whether even before August there was aggression by the Republic of Croatia on the area of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, and we didn't get an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you said "aggression," that is how I understood it, and that is how I replied. By "aggression" I understood you to mean a general offensive in the entire area. Before that there was a limited attack, an offensive on the Western Slavonia area in early May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this limited attack in May 1995 and then in August when the aggression took place in 1995, was there anything from this plan that is mentioned here and this plan that you took part in drafting, was anything from this plan something that actually occurred in the actual events on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the conversations and contacts and information that you had at the time, did President Milosevic have any political interest in having a document of this nature adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I also thought that he did. This was a very elegant solution. On the one hand, there were demands by the leadership of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, primarily Serbia, to assist them in preparations for the defence and in the execution of this defence of those territories if a general attack were to take place. On the other hand, Mr. Milosevic at the time was exposed to quite strong pressure from the opposition in Serbia. In Serbia at the time there was a very strongly formulated anti-war and isolationist movement, I could describe it like that. In the belief, that Serbia should not be waging war at all and this was something that most of the citizens believed. The development of this war plan would satisfy the requirements of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina leadership, and at the same time this plan as a top secret, top state secret, would remain concealed and no one could accuse him of supporting any kind of war option.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with this document, and now I would like to move to a different topic. Again we have to look at a document, this is P1023 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2023"]. It's a Prosecution exhibit. I hope, Your Honours, that you have been provided with a hard copy of the document. We are just going to be dealing with this document briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Court usher? Mr. Court usher? Mr. Court usher, can we show those documents to the Prosecution before you give them to the witness, please. Could you please show the Prosecution those -- the copies of those documents before you pass them on to the witness. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now returned to an older system of work that some in the courtroom used to like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my order from November 1993 dealing with the points that a combat report should contain, a combat report that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia -- a report in which we are informing the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia about all the important issues relating to the defence in the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment, just the document is recorded in the transcript at page 24, line 24, as being Prosecution Exhibit 2023. The correct number is Prosecution Exhibit 1023.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, why is this information that is required to be in the report important for the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia is the General Staff of the army that is along or right next to the zone that is engulfed by war. Also, it is the General Staff of a state that we considered to be our ethnic home state. This is the General Staff of the army that we were constantly asking things from. So it's quite normal that we should inform them about the situation. Had we had any other friendly General Staffs, we would probably have been sending similar information to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P1051. This is a Prosecution exhibit. This is now a document bearing the date the day after the date on the previous document. We can easily compare that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, first of all, can you tell me who drafted this document? You can look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to look. This is a document drafted by the operations organ of the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Krajina in co-operation with other organs of the Main Staff and which I signed in my capacity as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we are just going to go through a couple of entries. You are addressing the document to the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY, you can see that here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with this previous document in the context of noting or listing what a report should contain?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we thought that it would have more force if we addressed it also to the Supreme Defence Council, and this would go through the General Staff. We thought that they would have to submit it to the Supreme Defence Council which was also interested in being informed about the basic elements of the situation in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look, we don't have to read it out loud. If you can look at page 2 of the document where the heading is "Morale."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, I don't know what the page is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell me in terms of what is said in the document, why was this relevant to you at the time? And I would particularly like you to comment on the last sentence: "Soldiers are refusing to accept their salaries en masse even though that is for many of them the only source of living."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an accurate description of the situation as it was in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or rather, the situation in which members of the Serbian Army of the Krajina were, and the Serbian Army of the Krajina itself. And you can see where it says here the soldiers' salaries amount to 1 to 2 German marks. My salary at the time was about 3 marks. Borovo, that is an industrial plant in the eastern part of the area, in the Vukovar area, 40 to 50 marks. Vupik, that is an agricultural farm that manufactures agricultural products, 70 to 90 marks. The agricultural combines, 100 German marks or more. Some were actually receiving their salary in German marks. Municipal services, approximately 40 marks, and most were also receiving assistance in foodstuffs. So those who were working in any agricultural cooperative was paid the sum that was actually issued to 40 or 50 soldiers. Those who had uniforms, that was something -- those who were wearing uniforms refused to receive such a salary because they thought that that was something insulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how important were salaries to you officers at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salary was not important to me at all. I remember that my aide told me once, General, your salary has arrived, it's worth 12 marks, and I told him to go buy coffee for it. Next time he came and said that your salary has arrived and it's worth 6 marks. And I said very well. And then the following time my aide said to me, your salary is here and it's worth 3 marks, and I told him not to mention my salary anymore to me. That was the period of hyperinflation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard evidence before this Chamber that the highest hyperinflation was in the end of 1993. On the following page, this document discusses personnel and mobilisation issues. This is sub-item 2 and then item 3 underneath. And then the last paragraph just before the word "security." Could you please comment on this sentence, General. We need to point out that a large number of active servicemen has a status within FRY and that they are sending to the territory of Krajina would not amount to much, especially when it comes to reinforcements. Is this consistent with what you spoke of earlier so as not to waste too much time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The essence was that they had a proper status over there, they resolved all issues within the VJ, and they were not interested in coming to the territory of Krajina and being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are done with this document. We would like to see another similar document. Again this is a Prosecution Exhibit P1017.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again a similar report dated 21st of December, 1993. General, I see that you are looking at your watch, are you tired, do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us cover this document quickly. Do you recognise the signature, whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature is mine and the document was drafted by my Main Staff and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: This report is addressed differently. This one is addressed to the office of the president of the Republic of Serbia to President Slobodan Milosevic personally and simultaneously to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. My question is, why did you address this to President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have seen in the previous document that it was addressed to the Supreme Defence Council. We did it thinking that this document should reach Mr. Milosevic personally. And in this particular case, in this document, we addressed it specifically to Mr. Milosevic personally. As for Mr. Perisic, the document was addressed in this manner so that they wouldn't take it to the operations centre and place it among other documents without General Perisic seeing it at all. We thought that he should be aware of the basic elements of the situation given the position that he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard here ample evidence indicating that at the time Zoran Lilic was president of the Supreme Defence Council who was president of Serbia at the time. So I'm asking you this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rather, Mr. Lilic was president of Yugoslavia at the time -- interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I would like to know why it was important for you for Mr. Milosevic, president of Serbia to receive this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic frequently when I addressed him as Mr. President said to me we have only one president, those are the words that he said to me. And based on that, and based on my understanding of the situation and everything I had seen, it was clear to me that the real political authority was actually Mr. Milosevic and not Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this first part where they analyse enemy, could you please comment on this bit that begins with the following words: "In the autonomous region of Western Bosnia..." Would you please read this paragraph to yourself, and then I will ask you why in your view this portion containing the analysis of the enemy, why it was important for you to use this portion to inform Milosevic and Perisic about what was happening in the autonomous region of Western Bosnia? Remember during the first day of your testimony we drew it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the survival of the RSK and also for the activity of the RSK army, this region was very significant. It was significant because the existence of enemy forces in that area meant that our three corps had front line back to back. What is written here is quite interesting when it comes to our interests and it has to do with the conflict between the forces of Fikret Abdic, who had declared this autonomous region on the one hand, and the forces which remained loyal to Alija Izetbegovic within the 5th Corps on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to turn to page 3 in B/C/S. And it's right above the segment headed "Co-operation with UNPROFOR." And the paragraph begins with the words: "When it comes to the situation concerning the elections in the RSK ..." Do you see that General? That's page 3, the top part of page 3. Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain it to us without us actually reading it. What was actually happening at the time, when did these elections in the RSK actually take place, and what is it all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated 21st of December 1993, after the first round of elections for the office of the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was that period of time. The candidates were Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic. Mr. Martic received fewer votes than he expected after the first round. He believed, and he also tried to inform people in Belgrade in top positions, people in Serbia, that it was my fault as well as the fault of minister of defence, Admiral Rakic, and commanders of two corps, Banja Corps and another corps, rather the 7th and the 39th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how come he believed that it was your fault, would you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was caused by the fact that Mr. Martic had requested that I, Main Staff, and the commands of the formations in the depth of the territory of RSK all support his candidacy. And I refused to do that because within the RSK Army, some supported Babic and some supported Martic. I was not a commander and I could not put myself in the position where I would command only those people who supported Martic, and it was absolutely offensive to me for somebody to treat the army and the Main Staff who were supposed to take care of the fate of the people during the war to treat them as a political tool. The army always had a president at the top, this is how the constitution regulated it, and the army should not opt for any candidate in the elections. This was simply not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you just told us, did it affect your career at the position you held at the time, commander of the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a career. It was one great misfortune, not a really great successful career. But in the second round when Mr. Martic was finally elected, he expressed that he mistrusted me and one day he simply declared that he would remove me from office, even though according to the constitution only the parliament of the RSK could remove the commander of the army from that position. However, I did not want to play a role in creating any divisions or in deterioration of the situation in the Army of the RSK, and I wanted everything to be based on objective and realistic assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, who was appointed commander of the Army of the RSK after you had been removed from that position?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Celeketic who did not originally hail from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of President Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What position did General Celeketic hold prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed commander of the 18th Corps in Western Slavonia by way of my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you know, what was his record as commander of the corps while you were his superior?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Celeketic was subordinated to me as a lieutenant-colonel, even in the period of the Yugoslav People's Army when I was a commander Chief of Staff and he was -- rather, I was commander of the corps and he was Chief of Staff while we served in Koprivica. And when he served as commander of the corps, the position to which I appointed him, he did not exhibit any special qualities because he was not in a position to exhibit anything that would distinguish him. In my view, he was appointed to replace me in order to obediently follow instructions of the new president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did you learn at that time or later what position President Milosevic had in relation to your removal?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days after the announcement on my dismissal on the part of Mr. Martic, we were invited by Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Martic and Minister Rakic and I, minister of the defence, Admiral Rakic. He said a lot of things to Mr. Martic, using in reference to General Celeketic terms which would not be gentlemanly for me to repeat here, and the gist of it was revert to the previous state, what kind of rubbish are you doing, undo what you've just done. And so we went back to Knin, but the next morning this no longer held. A change had happened overnight and Mr. Milosevic kept quiet, and after a couple of days he asked me whether I wanted to become minister of defence. I refused to sit at government sessions which took longer than the sessions here in this courtroom. So it was decided that I become deputy and assistant supreme commander for strategic national defence and international relations, and the decision was based on the fact, among other things, that I believed that the situation we found ourselves in should be resolved through negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which government did Mr. Milosevic want you to become a minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was Mr. Milosevic's wish; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's go through another document with the witness. That would be P2156. I can see that it has appeared on the screen, but let's continue with this method regardless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an aide-memoire for co-ordination for the General Staff of the VJ for the 19th of November 1993. I'm revisiting a topic that we discussed yesterday. We are going to go through this document very quickly because I believe that it speaks for itself. On page 2 of this document, there is a heading: "Analysis of the Achievement of Tasks." "Since the last co-ordinating meeting, there are tasks which have been achieved and those which have not." Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, those tasks which had been achieved, how important were those for you at the moment in terms of what you received?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of what you can see written here, first of all, these are routine operative reporting. We saw a couple of examples of that a couple of minutes ago. One automatic telephone switchboard was repaired. Two technicians, some communications equipment, tactical radio stations for communication between battalions and companies were delivered, then three or four Galeb aircraft which are training aircraft, but could be used for reconnaissance and air support to very low extent. And then anti-aircraft motorised self-propelled artillery pieces. They were repaired and delivered, but since you do not have a command facility, you can treat those pieces as junk iron. Then some equipment was delivered which was the sum total of everything we got but the equipment for the operations centre for the control of the territory for air surveillance and guidance, nothing of the sort was delivered while I was commander there. And then there were 50 recruits sent to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that's irrelevant. He wants to explain something further.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that this was insignificant, part of the battalion for anti-aircraft defence, it is insignificant because, as you can see under B, tasks which have not been achieved then in the next row with respect to air surveillance identification, the following has not been achieved, radar of this type, some other types of radar, communications equipment for units to maintain air surveillance and to guide our anti-aircraft fire. This has not been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you that those radar systems were subsequently delivered?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge. To the best of my knowledge what was necessary for the missile battalion was delivered subsequently just for one battery. This is a medium range system which can be used to defend a small area occupied by a single unit or a small portion of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip some text until the item 5, the situation in the territory. What is discussed here is an extreme wing of the SDS monarchist who invite a revival of the Chetnik movement and advocate attacks against the former JNA members. I would like you to explain this segment. Why was it important for to you include this in the report to be discussed at such co-ordination meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We deemed this important so that both the VJ and President Milosevic be informed about attempts to organise paramilitary units. In other words, to create armed units outside the SVK which would use -- be used to support the certain politicians. We had precise assessment about those attempts. They tried to arrest certain people but there was no political support for such arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was -- where there was a dearth of political support in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or in Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last thing I'd like to elicit a comment from you about, it's not the last one but it's under item 6, sub-item (4) "communications," it contains quite a lot of technical gobbledegook. And there is on the next page a column "requests." Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to hear, do you recall whether those things which were requisitioned here were delivered by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not received while I was commander of the SVK. And what is requested here are tactical communications systems which means communications within a switchboard or communications between companies and battalions or for communications at positions of artilleries, except for the teleprinter which could be used for communications between a corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try to obtain important communications equipment in some other ways?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we had money, the Main Staff, not particularly I, bought the most up to date telecommunications equipment abroad, first and foremost for radio surveillance and sophisticated electronic systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you two questions. How did you get the money and what kind of systems are you referring to, just the labels or the titles?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army seised contraband cigarettes, and the proceeds, and I'll remember that well, were used to buy topnotch electronic surveillance, wire-tapping equipment, and the most up-to-date GPS equipment for our scouts for reconnaissance deep into enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is a similar type. It's an aide-memoire for the co-ordination meeting on the 17th of December, 1993. That would be P317 for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let's take a look at page 3 of the document. Analysis of the achieved tasks since the last co-ordination meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be below the Roman numeral I for your benefit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the achieved results, and it says here: "Utilisation plans had been drafted up to the level of corps." What does this mean? What has been achieved up to the corps level?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a joint war plan had been drafted, we updated our war plan at the Main Staff level to the extent necessary by the modifications of the joint war plan and its schedules, meaning the entirety of the joint war plan. However, at the corps levels and lower, we did not draft the war plan. If you wish me to explain, it was not done because we never found out which specific units would be coming to our territory and because the commanders of those units, which is customary procedure, inevitable procedure, was supposed to come to the zone where they would have to be located in accordance with their war deployment, and I mean those VJ units. They never arrived to those locations, and for that reason we did not elaborate and draft those plans. I simply did not dare issue such a task to avoid rumours about treason, about fraud, et cetera. I thought if I'm sure that nobody is going to come, let's not draft any such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue. I'm trying to speed up the proceedings. Under B, tasks not realised. And under C, tasks which have been presented at the previous co-ordinating level as not achieved, have not been achieved in the meantime, especially highlighting the problem with respect to rear guard supplies, and further on conclusions, it is stated: "As priorities we express the realisation of tasks, in terms of logistics and rather guard action, particularly supply of ammunition and spare parts." Could you please explain those entries?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, it means what is stated here. A previously expressed requests was not heeded and was not heeded for the second time round. No ammunition and no spare parts that we had requested have been delivered up to that point for our equipment, for our combat vehicles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be the right time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, if it's convenient to you. Thank you very much, and we'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I have a question to follow up on what we did in the previous session. In the period after the Medak pocket operation in September 1993 and all the way up until Operation Flash which was in May of 1995, were there any active combat operations, if I may call them that, to your knowledge in which the Army of SVK participated?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was partial engagement of the Army of SVK in the area of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that throughout this period or just during some time within this period, which is quite extensive?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of the reports that we saw here, it was mentioned that there was partial support to the forces of Fikret Abdic in the operations against the forces loyal to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was, was it for the entire period or was it for a limited time during this extensive period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was limited to the late fall of 1993 and also in winter between -- in winter of 1993 to 1994 with even fewer forces. These were operations limited to occasional artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These operations, these activities, did they cause additional depletion of resources of SVK in that period after the Medak pocket operation until Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no significant reduction in resources because there was no significant use of ammunition, to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us go back to the document. General, could we see item 6, mobilisation and personnel matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in English that's page 8 and 9 in the document before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the beginning we see "accomplished tasks," and they say, "The creation of the 40th Personnel Centre is underway." General, we need the heading "Mobilisation and Personnel Matters."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the page where there is a graph, on the page ahead of the graph. It's not a page we see on the screen now. I think it's two pages further down. I did initially say page 6, but it was my mistake. Thank you. The first sentence in this subsection reads: "The creation of the 40th Personnel Centre is underway. It will deal with the replenishment of the SVK, the Army of RSK." Let me ask you briefly, have you heard of these personnel centres, and where were they created? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th and the 40th Personnel Centres were established within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you seen, have you had occasion to see enactments on the creation of these personnel centres also regulating how they were to function?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how were you informed about the tasks of these centres?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The creation of the 40th Personnel Centre which dealt with the issues of replenishment of the Serbian Army of Krajina with active servicemen, that is to say professional officers and non-commissioned officers who used to be members of the Yugoslav People's Army came as a result of our request to establish such centres. The creation of this separate organ within the General Staff of the VJ meant that the General Staff of the VJ started dealing with this problem in an organised manner; that is to say, that people were engaged, were hired, to have an overview of the situation, survey so to speak of the situation, and also have records concerning the deployment of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you mention several times that there were no proper records of personnel. Why was it important in your view to have records on personnel and what did the personnel centres have do with these records?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic problem was that when it came to certain people, you simply did not know their whereabouts. Some left the Army of RSK saying that they needed to go back to their establishment position within the Army of Yugoslavia, within the VJ. However, whether they had the establishment position or not, whether they did indeed serve in one army or the other army during a certain period of time, those were outstanding issues and we simply had no records concerning them. Another goal that we wanted to accomplish by way of these centres was to have an exact accurate information as to the availability of such personnel. We also wanted to make it possible for those who were members of the SVK to have a place where they could go, to have an organ where they could go to regulate certain issues concerning their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at the end of the page under D, we see "personnel replenishment," "personnel reinforcement." I think that this part of the document speaks for itself, but let me put this question to you: With the establishment of personnel centres, the influx of the officers of the VJ who went to SVK, did it increase, did it stagnate, or did it -- or was there a reduction in the influx in the following period of time? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the initial period of stagnation, there was a reduction in the number of such personnel. However, the numbers seemed to be -- the numbers seemed to be maintained at the same level. However, that was just a matter of appearance, and you can see it on the last page of this document. Some of the people listed here, we simply didn't have them, and the people that did come to us were older and we didn't need them. We needed people who could serve as commanders of platoons and commanders of companies and such people never came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did you fill such positions in your army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to platoon commanders and company commanders, people who were soldiers, who were sergeants and non-commissioned officers of the former JNA, and who served in that territory in that area as soldiers of the SVK, we used them to fill those positions. We used those who seemed to be more able than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who paid their salaries?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the most accurate answer to your question would be nobody because the 1 or 2 German marks that they were to receive never arrived, so essentially they did not receive their salaries at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason for them to leave their positions, to stop serving as soldiers of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reply to your question, Mr. Lukic, perhaps we should clarify one matter. The Serbian Army of Krajina was not a -- an army organised in the barracks. It was simply people under arms. We within the SVK, we never managed to turn it into a regular army. If we analyse all of its features, all of its characteristics without going into professional specifics, we will see that it was people under arms. It was not a professional army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are giving us an answer much broader than I was interested in, so let us stick to what Judge Moloto said earlier to us. And my question was quite simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you is from whom or from what authority did the 1 or 2 German marks come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So would you please answer my question. The fact that salaries were so low and that they were seldom paid, did that prompt them to leave the SVK, to go away?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us look at another entry from this document concerning co-ordination, and it has to do with logistics, and that would be on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of that report, which, Your Honours, is page 9 in your copies. Or rather, 13, I apologise. They speak about fuel reserves. I think it was on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The page is marked as page 8 on the paper and it says "with completely depleted fuel reserves..." do you see that? Would you please read that paragraph to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you can follow, Your Honours, that is the last paragraph in this section and that begins with the words "with completely depleted fuel reserves, an inability to resupply..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you reacted -- or rather it says here you reacted to this by banning any further fuel distribution. So who was it who banned this further fuel distribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fuel that was processed in the Pancevo refinery arrived in the territory of RSK as processed fuel, and was stored in fuel warehouses of the Army of Yugoslavia in Bubanj Potok which is near Belgrade. After we had used up our fuel, which was recorded as our fuel, we had simply none left. And the previous arrangements made by logistics people was that they would give us some of their supplies and then once the new fuel arrived, we would give it back to them. And it is obvious that the logistics people of the VJ simply did not think of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with this document. Before I move to the next document I want to ask you this: General, was there co-operation between the intelligence organs of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, the Army of Yugoslavia, and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I'm not able to definitely say that it did not exist, you could say that it did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
